primary_citation.popular_name: DVPA Ex Parte Enjoinable Behaviors (incl. coercive control)

subdivision_a_enjoinable_behaviors.verbatim: The court may issue an ex parte order enjoining a party from molesting, attacking, striking, stalking, threatening, sexually assaulting, battering, credibly impersonating as described in Section 528.5 of the Penal Code, falsely personating as described in Section 529 of the Penal Code, harassing, telephoning, including, but not limited to, making annoying telephone calls as described in Section 653m of the Penal Code, destroying personal property, contacting, either directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise, coming within a specified distance of, or disturbing the peace of the other party, and, in the discretion of the court, on a showing of good cause, of other named family or household members.
enjoinable_behavior_list: telephoning (incl. annoying calls per Penal Code § 653m)
contacting (directly or indirectly, by mail or otherwise)
coming within a specified distance of
disturbing the peace of the other party
subdivision_a_enjoinable_behaviors.extension_to_other_named_persons: On a showing of good cause, the court may extend these prohibitions to other named family or household members

subdivision_b_animal_welfare.verbatim: On a showing of good cause, the court may include in a protective order a grant to the petitioner of the exclusive care, possession, or control of any animal owned, possessed, leased, kept, or held by either the petitioner or the respondent or a minor child residing in the residence or household of either the petitioner or the respondent. The court may order the respondent to stay away from the animal and forbid the respondent from taking, transferring, encumbering, concealing, molesting, attacking, striking, threatening, harming, or otherwise disposing of the animal.

subdivision_c_disturbing_the_peace_defin.verbatim_preamble: As used in subdivision (a), 'disturbing the peace of the other party' refers to conduct that, based on the totality of the circumstances, destroys the mental or emotional calm of the other party. This conduct may be committed directly or indirectly, including through the use of a third party, and by any method or through any means including, but not limited to, telephone, online accounts, text messages, internet-connected devices, including connected devices as defined in Section 22948.30 of the Business and Professions Code, or other electronic technologies. This conduct includes, but is not limited to, coercive control, which is a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty.
subdivision_c_disturbing_the_peace_defin.doctrinal_significance: This is the load-bearing expansion. 'Disturbing the peace' is now defined to include (1) totality-of-the-circumstances analysis, (2) direct OR indirect conduct, (3) conduct THROUGH A THIRD PARTY, (4) conduct via any method including electronic, (5) coercive control as a pattern. The 'through a third party' language is the doctrinal capture for orchestration patterns where the named respondent acts via intermediaries.
coercive_control_examples_verbatim: (1) Isolating the other party from friends, relatives, or other sources of support.
(2) Depriving the other party of basic necessities.
(3) Controlling, regulating, or monitoring the other party's movements, communications, daily behavior, finances, economic resources, or access to services.

(4) Compelling the other party by force, threat of force, or intimidation, including threats based on actual or suspected immigration status, to engage in conduct from which the other party has a right to abstain or to abstain from conduct in which the other party has a right to engage.

(5) Engaging in reproductive coercion, which consists of control over the reproductive autonomy of another through force, threat of force, or intimidation, and may include, but is not limited to, unreasonably pressuring the other party to become pregnant, deliberately interfering with contraception use or access to reproductive health information, or using coercive tactics to control, or attempt to control, pregnancy outcomes.

subdivision_d_non_limiting_clause.verbatim: This section does not limit any remedies available under this act or any other provision of law.

factor_audits.factor_id: (c) Disturbing the peace via third party — THE LOAD-BEARING NEW THEORY
factor_audits.what_the_statute_provides: The 2025 SB 50 amendment to § 6320(c) defines 'disturbing the peace' to include conduct committed 'directly or indirectly, including through the use of a third party.' This is the explicit statutory capture for orchestration patterns.
factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: Per project_familylaw_orchestration.md, the documented pattern is that Christina acts in concert with Ann Hillberg (mother, state police/emergency dispatcher 2008-2015) who: (1) stages unauthorized civil standbys to generate police reports against the steward, (2) makes 911 calls using dispatcher language designed to trigger specific official responses, (3) coordinates the movement of the child Cole across jurisdictions, (4) orchestrates triple filings with grandparent visitation petitions. Per project_ryan_mcclaran_it.md, the pattern also includes IT-mediated harassment via SIM swaps and proxy communication networks.
factor_audits.audit_question: Does the documented Christina-Hillberg-McClaran orchestration pattern fall within the § 6320(c) 'through a third party' / 'by any method or through any means' definition of disturbing the peace?
factor_audits.audit_status: CRITICAL — POTENTIALLY ENABLES A NEW AFFIRMATIVE DVRO PETITION. The 2025 amendment (effective 2026-01-01) explicitly enjoins third-party-orchestrated conduct. The documented orchestration pattern in the case file is structurally a § 6320(c) violation. A new DVRO petition by the steward against Christina, naming Hillberg and others as 'other named family or household members' under the (a) extension clause, may be statutorily supportable. This would be a fresh affirmative theory rather than a defensive posture against the Marin DVRO.

factor_audits.what_the_record_shows: The documented pattern includes isolating Cole from the steward across multiple periods (the 2023-06-22 Benicia apartment incident; the 2025-07-08 transfer-window handoff; the 2025-07-13 to 2025-07-17 Marin removal). Per project_communications_fraud.md and project_ryan_mcclaran_it.md, the SIM swap pattern, proxy communication network, and physical-proximity device-access requirements documented in the case file are structurally controlling/monitoring/regulating the steward's communications and access to services. steward_case_relevance_audit.audit_summary: ONE CRITICAL audit item: § 6320(c) third-party orchestration capture. The 2025 SB 50 amendment to § 6320(c) explicitly enjoins conduct committed 'through a third party' and defines coercive control as 'a pattern of behavior that in purpose or effect unreasonably interferes with a person's free will and personal liberty.' The documented Christina-Hillberg-McClaran orchestration pattern in the case file is structurally a § 6320(c) violation. **This may enable a new affirmative DVRO petition by the steward against Christina based on the entire 16-year pattern, not just discrete incidents.** This is a fresh strategic option distinct from defending the Marin FL0002067 or filing a federal § 1983 complaint. Steward review required to determine whether to pursue this affirmative theory.
